claim: A chemogenetic approach using CRISPR-Cas9 screening was employed to discover novel cellular networks that regulate cell cycle progression.
source: We employed a chemogenetic approach to discover novel cellular networks that regulate cell cycle progression.
evidence: The abstract directly states the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The chemogenetic approach uncovered functional clusters of genes that altered sensitivity of cells to inhibitors of the G1/S transition.
source: This approach uncovered functional clusters of genes that altered sensitivity of cells to inhibitors of the G1/S transition.
evidence: The abstract describes the results obtained from the chemogenetic screening approach.

claim: Mutation of components of the Polycomb Repressor Complex 2 rescued proliferation inhibition caused by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib.
source: Mutation of components of the Polycomb Repressor Complex 2 rescued proliferation inhibition caused by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib, but not to inhibitors of S phase or mitosis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the screen.

claim: Mutation of PRC2 components did not rescue proliferation inhibition caused by inhibitors of S phase or mitosis.
source: Mutation of components of the Polycomb Repressor Complex 2 rescued proliferation inhibition caused by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib, but not to inhibitors of S phase or mitosis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the specificity of the PRC2 effect to palbociclib.

claim: Mutation of the PRC2.1 accessory protein MTF2 rendered cells resistant to palbociclib treatment.
source: In addition to its core catalytic subunits, mutation of the PRC2.1 accessory protein MTF2, but not the PRC2.2 protein JARID2, rendered cells resistant to palbociclib treatment.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the differential effects of MTF2 and JARID2 mutations.

claim: Mutation of the PRC2.2 protein JARID2 did not render cells resistant to palbociclib treatment.
source: In addition to its core catalytic subunits, mutation of the PRC2.1 accessory protein MTF2, but not the PRC2.2 protein JARID2, rendered cells resistant to palbociclib treatment.
evidence: The abstract explicitly contrasts the effects of MTF2 and JARID2 mutations.

claim: PRC2.1 (MTF2), but not PRC2.2 (JARID2), is critical for promoting H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands genome-wide.
source: We found that PRC2.1 (MTF2), but not PRC2.2 (JARID2), was critical for promoting H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands genome-wide and in promoters.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from CUT&RUN experiments.

claim: PRC2.1 (MTF2), but not PRC2.2 (JARID2), is critical for promoting H3K27me3 deposition in promoters.
source: We found that PRC2.1 (MTF2), but not PRC2.2 (JARID2), was critical for promoting H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands genome-wide and in promoters.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from CUT&RUN experiments.

claim: The CpG islands in the promoter of CCND1 and CCND2 are targets of PRC2.1-mediated H3K27me3 deposition.
source: This included the CpG islands in the promoter of the CDK4/6 cyclins CCND1 and CCND2, and loss of MTF2 lead to upregulation of both CCND1 and CCND2.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies CCND1 and CCND2 promoters as targets.

claim: Loss of MTF2 leads to upregulation of both CCND1 and CCND2.
source: This included the CpG islands in the promoter of the CDK4/6 cyclins CCND1 and CCND2, and loss of MTF2 lead to upregulation of both CCND1 and CCND2.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this consequence of MTF2 loss.

claim: PRC2.1, but not PRC2.2, plays a role in antagonizing G1 progression in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).
source: Our results demonstrate a role for PRC2.1, but not PRC2.2, in antagonizing G1 progression in a diversity of cell linages, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), breast cancer, and immortalized cell lines.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding across multiple cell types.

claim: PRC2.1, but not PRC2.2, plays a role in antagonizing G1 progression in breast cancer.
source: Our results demonstrate a role for PRC2.1, but not PRC2.2, in antagonizing G1 progression in a diversity of cell linages, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), breast cancer, and immortalized cell lines.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding across multiple cell types.

claim: PRC2.1, but not PRC2.2, plays a role in antagonizing G1 progression in immortalized cell lines.
source: Our results demonstrate a role for PRC2.1, but not PRC2.2, in antagonizing G1 progression in a diversity of cell linages, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), breast cancer, and immortalized cell lines.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding across multiple cell types.

claim: Progression through the G1 phase of the cell cycle is the most highly regulated step in cellular division.
source: Progression through the G1 phase of the cell cycle is the most highly regulated step in cellular division.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Regulated progression through the cell cycle is crucial for normal cellular growth and organismal development.
source: Regulated progression through the cell cycle is crucial for normal cellular growth and organismal development (Ginzberg et al., 2015; Massagué, 2004; Bertoli et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Progression from G1 into S phase is the most highly regulated step of the cell cycle.
source: Progression from G1 into S phase is the most highly regulated step of the cell cycle, as initiating DNA replication commits a cell to divide and is frequently mutationally activated in tumors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with reasoning provided.

claim: Initiating DNA replication commits a cell to divide.
source: Progression from G1 into S phase is the most highly regulated step of the cell cycle, as initiating DNA replication commits a cell to divide and is frequently mutationally activated in tumors.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: The G1/S transition is frequently mutationally activated in tumors.
source: Progression from G1 into S phase is the most highly regulated step of the cell cycle, as initiating DNA replication commits a cell to divide and is frequently mutationally activated in tumors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: CDK4 and CDK6 play critical roles in promoting G1 progression through phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (RB1).
source: Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 4 (CDK4) and the related CDK6 (henceforth referred to collectively as CDK4/6) play critical roles in promoting G1 progression through phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (RB1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation of RB1 by CDK4/6 relieves RB1-mediated transcriptional repression of E2F transcription factors.
source: Phosphorylation relieves RB1-mediated transcriptional repression of E2F transcription factors, which are then competent to drive transcription of genes necessary for progression into S phase (Bertoli et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2020; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2005; Bracken et al., 2004).
evidence: This mechanism is described with supporting citations.

claim: E2F transcription factors drive transcription of genes necessary for progression into S phase.
source: Phosphorylation relieves RB1-mediated transcriptional repression of E2F transcription factors, which are then competent to drive transcription of genes necessary for progression into S phase (Bertoli et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2020; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2005; Bracken et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Palbociclib was the first FDA approved CDK4/6 inhibitor.
source: Palbociclib was the first FDA approved CDK4/6 inhibitor and highly efficacious in the treatment of HR+/HER2− breast cancers, followed by the structurally related molecules ribociclib and abemaciclib (Dickler et al., 2017; Morrison et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2018; Im et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact with supporting citations.

claim: Palbociclib is highly efficacious in the treatment of HR+/HER2− breast cancers.
source: Palbociclib was the first FDA approved CDK4/6 inhibitor and highly efficacious in the treatment of HR+/HER2− breast cancers, followed by the structurally related molecules ribociclib and abemaciclib (Dickler et al., 2017; Morrison et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2018; Im et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2022).
evidence: This clinical efficacy is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ribociclib and abemaciclib are structurally related to palbociclib.
source: Palbociclib was the first FDA approved CDK4/6 inhibitor and highly efficacious in the treatment of HR+/HER2− breast cancers, followed by the structurally related molecules ribociclib and abemaciclib (Dickler et al., 2017; Morrison et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2018; Im et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2022).
evidence: This structural relationship is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The classical model of G1 regulation has given way to a more complex model.
source: However, this classical model of G1 regulation has recently given way to a more complex model (Cappell et al., 2018; Cappell et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019), underscored by the complexity of genetic alterations that lead to resistance to treatment with CDK4/6 inhibitors (Rubin et al., 2020; Cappell et al., 2018; Cappell et al., 2016; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This evolution in understanding is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Genetic alterations that lead to resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors are complex.
source: However, this classical model of G1 regulation has recently given way to a more complex model (Cappell et al., 2018; Cappell et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019), underscored by the complexity of genetic alterations that lead to resistance to treatment with CDK4/6 inhibitors (Rubin et al., 2020; Cappell et al., 2018; Cappell et al., 2016; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This complexity is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) was initially identified in Drosophila as a developmental regulator that represses the expression of Hox genes.
source: The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) was initially identified in Drosophila as a developmental regulator that represses the expression of Hox genes (Lewis, 1978).
evidence: This historical discovery is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The PRC2 complex is conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: The PRC2 complex is conserved in throughout eukaryotes (Dumesic et al., 2015; Grimaud et al., 2006; Jamieson et al., 2013; Schuettengruber et al., 2017; Kuroda et al., 2020) and catalyzes the mono-, di-, and tri-methylation of Histone 3 Lysine 27 (referred to collectively as H3K27me3, the fully methylated form of H3K27) and thereby acts as a transcriptional repressor (Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This conservation is stated with supporting citations.

claim: PRC2 catalyzes the mono-, di-, and tri-methylation of Histone 3 Lysine 27 (H3K27me3).
source: The PRC2 complex is conserved in throughout eukaryotes (Dumesic et al., 2015; Grimaud et al., 2006; Jamieson et al., 2013; Schuettengruber et al., 2017; Kuroda et al., 2020) and catalyzes the mono-, di-, and tri-methylation of Histone 3 Lysine 27 (referred to collectively as H3K27me3, the fully methylated form of H3K27) and thereby acts as a transcriptional repressor (Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This enzymatic activity is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: PRC2 acts as a transcriptional repressor.
source: The PRC2 complex is conserved in throughout eukaryotes (Dumesic et al., 2015; Grimaud et al., 2006; Jamieson et al., 2013; Schuettengruber et al., 2017; Kuroda et al., 2020) and catalyzes the mono-, di-, and tri-methylation of Histone 3 Lysine 27 (referred to collectively as H3K27me3, the fully methylated form of H3K27) and thereby acts as a transcriptional repressor (Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This function is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The core PRC2 complex is composed of EED, SUZ12, and EZH2.
source: The core PRC2 complex is composed of a H3K27me3 'reader' EED, a scaffold protein SUZ12, and the catalytic subunit EZH2 (or the more poorly expressed and less catalytically active paralog EZH1; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This composition is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: EED is a H3K27me3 'reader' in the PRC2 complex.
source: The core PRC2 complex is composed of a H3K27me3 'reader' EED, a scaffold protein SUZ12, and the catalytic subunit EZH2 (or the more poorly expressed and less catalytically active paralog EZH1; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This function is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: SUZ12 is a scaffold protein in the PRC2 complex.
source: The core PRC2 complex is composed of a H3K27me3 'reader' EED, a scaffold protein SUZ12, and the catalytic subunit EZH2 (or the more poorly expressed and less catalytically active paralog EZH1; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This function is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: EZH2 is the catalytic subunit of the PRC2 complex.
source: The core PRC2 complex is composed of a H3K27me3 'reader' EED, a scaffold protein SUZ12, and the catalytic subunit EZH2 (or the more poorly expressed and less catalytically active paralog EZH1; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This function is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: EZH1 is a paralog of EZH2 that is more poorly expressed and less catalytically active.
source: The core PRC2 complex is composed of a H3K27me3 'reader' EED, a scaffold protein SUZ12, and the catalytic subunit EZH2 (or the more poorly expressed and less catalytically active paralog EZH1; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This relationship is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The core PRC2 complex is capable of catalyzing H3K27me3 deposition and chromatin association.
source: This core complex is capable of catalyzing H3K27me3 deposition and chromatin association, but how PRC2 achieves full spatiotemporal regulation of chromatin localization and catalytic activity has been an area of active investigation.
evidence: This capability is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Additional accessory factors modify the localization and enzymatic activity of PRC2 core components.
source: Recent studies have identified additional accessory factors that modify the localization and enzymatic activity of these core components (Hauri et al., 2016).
evidence: This finding is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The associated auxiliary factors define different PRC2 subcomplexes called PRC2.1 and PRC2.2.
source: The associated auxiliary factors define different PRC2 subcomplexes, which are called PRC2.1 and PRC2.2, based on the composition of the subunits associated with the core PRC2 complex (reviewed in van Mierlo et al., 2019; Piunti and Shilatifard, 2021).
evidence: This classification is stated with supporting citations to reviews.

claim: PRC2.1 consists of the core PRC2 subunits plus a Polycomb-like (PCL) protein (PHF1, MTF2, or PHF19) and either PALI1/2 or EPOP.
source: In addition to the core PRC2 subunits, PRC2.1 consists of two modules, one module containing a Polycomb-like (PCL) protein PHF1, MTF2, or PHF19 and a second module of either PALI1/2 or EPOP.
evidence: This composition is stated as established knowledge.

claim: PRC2.2 consists of the core PRC2 subunits in complex with both JARID2 and AEBP2.
source: The more homogenous PRC2.2 always consists of the core PRC2 subunits in complex with both JARID2 and AEBP2.
evidence: This composition is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The presence of a DNA-binding extended homology domain in each PCL protein has been proposed to recruit PRC2.1 to unmethylated CpG islands and establish H3K27me3.
source: Despite the lack of an a clear analogous sequence to the Polycomb Response Elements which promotes PRC2 chromatin association in Drosophila (Brown et al., 2018; De et al., 2020), the presence of a DNA-binding extended homology domain in each PCL protein has been proposed to recruit PRC2.1 to unmethylated CpG islands and establish H3K27me3 (Perino et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This proposed mechanism is stated with supporting citations.

claim: PRC2.2 localizes to sites utilizing pre-existing mono-ubiquitinated H2AK119 (H2AK119ub1), which is deposited by the PRC1 complex.
source: In contrast, PRC2.2 localizes to sites utilizing pre-existing mono-ubiquitinated H2AK119 (H2AK119ub1), which is deposited by the PRC1 complex (Barbour et al., 2020; Cooper et al., 2016; Kalb et al., 2014; Glancy et al., 2023), through a ubiquitin interaction motif contained within JARID2 (Cooper et al., 2016; Kalb et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2018; Kasinath et al., 2021).
evidence: This localization mechanism is stated with supporting citations.

claim: JARID2 contains a ubiquitin interaction motif that mediates PRC2.2 localization to H2AK119ub1 sites.
source: In contrast, PRC2.2 localizes to sites utilizing pre-existing mono-ubiquitinated H2AK119 (H2AK119ub1), which is deposited by the PRC1 complex (Barbour et al., 2020; Cooper et al., 2016; Kalb et al., 2014; Glancy et al., 2023), through a ubiquitin interaction motif contained within JARID2 (Cooper et al., 2016; Kalb et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2018; Kasinath et al., 2021).
evidence: This molecular detail is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Members of both PRC2.1 and PRC2.2 have been implicated as both positive and negative regulators of stem cell maintenance, differentiation, and cancer, depending on the cellular context.
source: Regardless of their specific roles in the propagation of H3K27me3 histone marks, members of both PRC2.1 and PRC2.2 have been implicated as both positive and negative regulators of stem cell maintenance, differentiation, and cancer, depending on the cellular context (Piunti and Shilatifard, 2021; Su et al., 2015; Shirato et al., 2009; Adhikari and Davie, 2018; Petracovici and Bonasio, 2021; Loh et al., 2021; Rothberg et al., 2018; Ngubo et al., 2023).
evidence: This context-dependent function is stated with supporting citations.

claim: All of the PRC2 core subunits (EZH2, SUZ12, and EED) have been shown to inhibit transcription of both positive and negative regulators of G1/S progression, including the CDK4/6 protein inhibitor p16.
source: All of the PRC2 core subunits (EZH2, SUZ12, and EED) have been shown to inhibit that transcription of both positive and negative regulators of G1/S progression, including the CDK4/6 protein inhibitor p16 (Bracken et al., 2007; Bracken et al., 2006; Bracken et al., 2003; Adhikari et al., 2019; Adhikari and Davie, 2020).
evidence: This regulatory function is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The Toronto Knockout Library was used for the CRISPR-Cas9 whole-genome screen.
source: We then performed a CRISPR–Cas9 whole-genome screen for each of the three inhibitors (Figure 1A) by introducing the Toronto Knockout Library (Hart et al., 2017) via lentiviral transduction into an HAP1 cell line constitutively expressing Cas9.
evidence: The methods section explicitly states the library used.

claim: The Toronto Knockout Library contains 70,948 guides targeting 18,053 protein-coding genes (4 guides/gene).
source: The library contains 70,948 guides, targeting 18,053 protein-coding genes (4 guides/gene).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the library composition.

claim: Cells were propagated in either DMSO (Mock) or in the presence of drug (Treated) for 18 days following puromycin selection.
source: Following puromycin selection for 2 days, cells were propagated in either DMSO (Mock) or in the presence of drug (Treated) for 18 days.
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the experimental timeline.

claim: A gene was considered significantly enriched or de-enriched if both the Loess-adjusted differential gene effect between mean Treated and Mock control was ±0.5 and the FDR <0.4.
source: A gene was considered as being significantly enriched or de-enriched in a given condition if both the Loess-adjusted differential gene effect between mean Treated and Mock control was ±0.5 and the and a false discovery rate (FDR) <0.4.
evidence: The methods section explicitly states the significance criteria.

claim: Inactivation of genes encoding members of the Fanconi Anemia pathway strongly sensitized cells to camptothecin.
source: For example, targeting of genes known to play roles in DNA damage repair (DDR) (Groelly et al., 2023; Su et al., 2020), including RAD54L, MUS81, and 16 proteins in the Fanconi Anemia pathway, strongly sensitized cells to camptothecin, which generates protein–DNA adducts (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: TOP1 is the molecular target of camptothecin.
source: The molecular target of camptothecin, TOP1 (Hsiang et al., 1985), is the most resistant gene in the camptothecin screen, as are proteins involved in p53 transcriptional regulation, such as TP53BP1 and STAGA members TAF2, TAF4, TAF5, TAF11, and TAF13 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation and reference to figure data.

claim: TOP1 is the most resistant gene in the camptothecin screen.
source: The molecular target of camptothecin, TOP1 (Hsiang et al., 1985), is the most resistant gene in the camptothecin screen, as are proteins involved in p53 transcriptional regulation, such as TP53BP1 and STAGA members TAF2, TAF4, TAF5, TAF11, and TAF13 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure data.

claim: Colchicine sensitized cells to the mutation of genes encoding proteins involved in mitotic spindle assembly, nuclear division and cytoskeletal assembly.
source: Similarly, colchicine sensitized cells to the mutation of genes encoding proteins involved in mitotic spindle assembly, nuclear division and cytoskeletal assembly, such as CLASP1, DLGAP5, and KNTC1 (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Inactivation of genes involved in the adaptive immune system resulted in sensitivity to colchicine.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of genes involved in the adaptive immune system, such as BIRC6, UBA5, and USP14, also resulted in sensitivity to colchicine.
evidence: The results section states this unexpected finding.

claim: Colchicine is used clinically as an immunomodulator in the treatment of gout.
source: This observation is intriguing, as colchicine is used clinically as an immunomodulator in the treatment of gout (Dalbeth et al., 2014).
evidence: This clinical use is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: CCNE1 ranked as the 2nd most important gene for palbociclib sensitivity.
source: CCNE1, CDK6, CDK2, CCND2, and CCND1, all of which are integral to promoting the G1/S phase transition, ranked as the 2nd, 24th, 27th, 29th, and 46th most important genes for palbociclib sensitivity, respectively (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: The results section states this ranking with reference to figures.

claim: CDK6 ranked as the 24th most important gene for palbociclib sensitivity.
source: CCNE1, CDK6, CDK2, CCND2, and CCND1, all of which are integral to promoting the G1/S phase transition, ranked as the 2nd, 24th, 27th, 29th, and 46th most important genes for palbociclib sensitivity, respectively (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: The results section states this ranking with reference to figures.

claim: CDK2 ranked as the 27th most important gene for palbociclib sensitivity.
source: CCNE1, CDK6, CDK2, CCND2, and CCND1, all of which are integral to promoting the G1/S phase transition, ranked as the 2nd, 24th, 27th, 29th, and 46th most important genes for palbociclib sensitivity, respectively (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: The results section states this ranking with reference to figures.

claim: CCND2 ranked as the 29th most important gene for palbociclib sensitivity.
source: CCNE1, CDK6, CDK2, CCND2, and CCND1, all of which are integral to promoting the G1/S phase transition, ranked as the 2nd, 24th, 27th, 29th, and 46th most important genes for palbociclib sensitivity, respectively (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: The results section states this ranking with reference to figures.

claim: CCND1 ranked as the 46th most important gene for palbociclib sensitivity.
source: CCNE1, CDK6, CDK2, CCND2, and CCND1, all of which are integral to promoting the G1/S phase transition, ranked as the 2nd, 24th, 27th, 29th, and 46th most important genes for palbociclib sensitivity, respectively (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: The results section states this ranking with reference to figures.

claim: Cells with sgRNAs targeting RB1 displayed substantial resistance to palbociclib.
source: Similarly, cells with sgRNAs targeting RB1, whose phosphorylation by CDK4/6 is a critical step in G1 progression, displayed substantial resistance to palbociclib.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: The majority of genes that conferred either sensitivity or resistance were specific to only one cell cycle inhibitor, with little overlap between the multiple conditions.
source: The majority of genes that conferred either sensitivity or resistance were specific to only one cell cycle inhibitor, with little overlap between the multiple conditions, suggesting that we identified genes that play roles in distinct biological processes (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Only 13 genes resulted in sensitivity in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition.
source: We found that only 13 and 20 genes resulted in sensitivity or resistance, respectively, in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition, and excluded from any further analysis (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Only 20 genes resulted in resistance in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition.
source: We found that only 13 and 20 genes resulted in sensitivity or resistance, respectively, in all the compounds tested and were deemed non-specific to a given condition, and excluded from any further analysis (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Loss of genes involved in chromatin structure and the metabolism of RNA conferred resistance to camptothecin.
source: In contrast, sgRNAs targeting of genes involved in RNA metabolism and chromatin organization increased resistance to this drug (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Inactivation of genes encoding members of the KICSTOR complex resulted in de-enrichment in the camptothecin screen.
source: In addition to DDR genes, Metascape and STRING analysis of the results of our camptothecin treatment revealed de-enrichment for sgRNAs targeting genes encoding members of the KICSTOR complex (KPTN, SZT2, ITFG2, and KICS2), which negatively regulates the mTOR pathway.
evidence: The results section states this finding from pathway analysis.

claim: The KICSTOR complex negatively regulates the mTOR pathway.
source: In addition to DDR genes, Metascape and STRING analysis of the results of our camptothecin treatment revealed de-enrichment for sgRNAs targeting genes encoding members of the KICSTOR complex (KPTN, SZT2, ITFG2, and KICS2), which negatively regulates the mTOR pathway.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the KICSTOR complex.

claim: mTOR is involved in attenuating the DDR response through phosphorylation of RNF168, leading to its degradation.
source: It has been suggested that mTOR is involved in attenuating the DDR response through phosphorylation of RNF168, leading to its degradation (Xie et al., 2018), which could provide one explanation of the observed sensitivity.
evidence: This mechanism is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response.
source: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response (DEPDC5 TSC1, SZT2, and NPRL2) and mRNA splicing (SNRPB2, SF3B2, PPIL1, RBM22, and DHX35), while mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking (VPS16, VPS18, VPS29, VPS41, VPS51, and VPS52) or encode members of the Mediator complex (CCNC, CDK8, and MED26, MED1, MED7, MED12, MED18, and MED11) attenuated the cellular response to the drug.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking attenuated the cellular response to colchicine.
source: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response (DEPDC5 TSC1, SZT2, and NPRL2) and mRNA splicing (SNRPB2, SF3B2, PPIL1, RBM22, and DHX35), while mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking (VPS16, VPS18, VPS29, VPS41, VPS51, and VPS52) or encode members of the Mediator complex (CCNC, CDK8, and MED26, MED1, MED7, MED12, MED18, and MED11) attenuated the cellular response to the drug.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Mutation of genes encoding members of the Mediator complex attenuated the cellular response to colchicine.
source: Genes whose inactivation enhanced sensitivity to colchicine included those involved in the amino acid starvation response (DEPDC5 TSC1, SZT2, and NPRL2) and mRNA splicing (SNRPB2, SF3B2, PPIL1, RBM22, and DHX35), while mutation of genes that control vesicle trafficking (VPS16, VPS18, VPS29, VPS41, VPS51, and VPS52) or encode members of the Mediator complex (CCNC, CDK8, and MED26, MED1, MED7, MED12, MED18, and MED11) attenuated the cellular response to the drug.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Inactivation of genes encoding members of the Fanconi Anemia complex resulted in resistance to colchicine.
source: Unexpectedly, inactivation of genes encoding members of the TP53 signaling pathway (TFDP1 and HIPK2), SAGA H3 acetylation complex components (KAT2A, TRRAP, TADA3, TAF5L, TADA2B, SGF29, and TADA1), and the Fanconi Anemia complex (FANCA, FANCC, FANCE, FANCF, FANCG, FANCL, and FAAP100), all implicated in DDR, resulted in resistance to colchicine (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The results section states this unexpected finding with reference to figures.

claim: Sensitivity to palbociclib was enhanced in cells expressing sgRNAs targeting H4 acetylation, positive regulators of Pol II transcription and regulators of DDR.
source: Sensitivity to palbociclib was enhanced in cells expressing sgRNAs targeting H4 acetylation, positive regulators of Pol II transcription and regulators of DDR (Figure 3A, B), although this sensitivity was much weaker than that seen with DNA damaging agents.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Long-term treatment with palbociclib induces DNA damage.
source: This observation is consistent with long-term treatment with palbociclib inducing DNA damage, as has been suggested by a number of recent publications (Crozier et al., 2023; Crozier et al., 2022; Wilson et al., 2023).
evidence: This interpretation is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Inactivation of members of the SIN3 histone deacetylase complex resulted in palbociclib sensitivity.
source: Inactivation of members of the SIN3 histone deacetylase (SIN3B, SINHCAF, and ARID4B), the NuA4 histone acetyltransferase (ING3, DMAP1, MORF4L2, YEATS4, and VPS73), the STAGA histone acetyltransferase (KAT2A, TADA1, TADA2B, TAF5L, and SUPT20H), and the Mediator (MED13, MED25, MED10, MED15, TAF7, TAG13, and CCNC) complexes all resulted in palbociclib sensitivity (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Almost 25% (170 out of 689) of the genes whose mutation conferred unique resistance to palbociclib have terms associated with mitochondrial respiratory chain complex assembly, ATP synthesis, or mitochondrial gene expression.
source: Strikingly, almost 25% (170 out of the 689) of the genes whose mutation conferred unique resistance to palbociclib have terms associated with mitochondrial respiratory chain complex assembly, ATP synthesis, or mitochondrial gene expression.
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: Cells exposed to rotenone, TTFA, and oligomycin displayed dose-dependent, positive proliferation interactions when treated in combination with palbociclib.
source: Cells exposed to rotenone, TTFA, and oligomycin displayed dose-dependent, positive proliferation interactions when treated in combination with palbociclib (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), indicating that combined inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation and CDK4/6 activity mutually rescue the proliferation defect imposed by agents targeting the other process.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib.
source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures and supplementary data.

claim: EZH2 was the eighth strongest resistance hit to palbociclib out of 18,053 genes examined.
source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section states this ranking.

claim: SUZ12 was the fourth strongest resistance hit to palbociclib out of 18,053 genes examined.
source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section states this ranking.

claim: EED was the third strongest resistance hit to palbociclib out of 18,053 genes examined.
source: Intriguingly, inactivation of EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, the three core members of the PRC2 complex, resulted in profound resistance to palbociclib, being the eighth, fourth, and third strongest resistance hits out of the 18,053 genes examined when ranked by the score of differential effect (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section states this ranking.

claim: Mutation of RBBP7 de-sensitized cells to palbociclib, but to a more modest extent than core PRC2 components.
source: Mutation of RBBP7, which associates with the core PRC2 complex (Schuettengruber et al., 2017) along with a number of histone deacetylases (De La Fuente, 2014), also de-sensitized cells to palbociclib, but to a more modest extent.
evidence: The results section states this finding with supporting citations.

claim: Inactivation of RING1, RNF2, and PCGF6 displayed resistance to palbociclib.
source: Satisfyingly, inactivation of RING1, RNF2, and PCGF6, which are members of PRC1, also displayed resistance to palbociclib.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: The PRC1 complex contains a ubiquitin ligase that works in concert with PRC2 through H2AK119ub1 deposition.
source: The PRC1 complex contains a ubiquitin ligase that works in concert with PRC2 through H2AK119ub1 deposition, a histone mark that influences both PRC2 chromatin localization and catalytic activity (Barbour et al., 2020; Kalb et al., 2014).
evidence: This mechanism is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Inactivation of genes encoding OGT, ASXL1, and HAT1 resulted in sensitivity to palbociclib.
source: In contrast, inactivation of genes encoding OGT, ASXL1, and HAT1, which are members of the H2AK119ub1 deubiquitinase complex that opposes PRC2-mediated gene repression (Chittock et al., 2017), resulted in sensitivity to palbociclib (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section states this finding with a supporting citation and reference to figure.

claim: No component of any PRC1 or PRC2 core complex displayed significant resistance or sensitivity to camptothecin and colchicine.
source: Importantly, no component of any PRC1 or PRC2 core complex displayed significant resistance or sensitivity to camptothecin and colchicine in our chemogenetic screens (Figure 4C), implicating PRC2 in the regulation of G1 specifically, and not to other phases of the cell cycle or the DNA damage response pathway.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure.

claim: Cells treated with increasing doses of GSK126 withstood palbociclib-induced proliferation suppression.
source: After 9 days of drug combination treatments, we found that cells treated with increasing doses of GSK126 withstood palbociclib-induced proliferation suppression (Figure 4D), though even the highest dose utilized of 5 µM GSK126 had some synergistic effects with low doses of palbociclib.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing the data.

claim: Mutation of the PRC2.1 complex members PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, and EPOP/C17orf96 all display significant resistance to palbociclib.
source: Mutation of the PRC2.1 complex members PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, and EPOP/C17orf96 all display significant resistance to palbociclib, with MTF2 being the strongest of these (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: MTF2 is the strongest PRC2.1 component conferring resistance to palbociclib.
source: Mutation of the PRC2.1 complex members PHF1, MTF2, PHF19, and EPOP/C17orf96 all display significant resistance to palbociclib, with MTF2 being the strongest of these (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Targeting the gene encoding AEBP2 resulted in enhanced palbociclib sensitivity.
source: Conversely, targeting the genes encoding the PRC2.2-specific accessory proteins AEBP2 or JARID2 resulted in enhanced or neutral palbociclib sensitivity, respectively.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Targeting the gene encoding JARID2 resulted in neutral palbociclib sensitivity.
source: Conversely, targeting the genes encoding the PRC2.2-specific accessory proteins AEBP2 or JARID2 resulted in enhanced or neutral palbociclib sensitivity, respectively.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Pools containing sgRNAs against EZH2, SUZ12, EED, and MTF2 all displayed resistance to palbociclib.
source: Pools containing sgRNAs against EZH2, SUZ12, EED, and MTF2 all displayed resistance to palbociclib, similar to the level observed with sgRNAs targeting RB1, our positive control for palbociclib-induced proliferation defects (Figure 4E).
evidence: The results section states this validation finding with reference to figure.

claim: sgRNAs targeting PRC2.2 components showed a slight, but statistically significant reduction in proliferation in palbociclib over the 18-day assay.
source: Conversely, compared with the dramatic reduction seen in pools transduced with CCNE1 sgRNAs, our positive control for enhanced palbociclib sensitivity CCNE1, sgRNAs targeting PRC2.2 components showed a slight, but statistically signification reduction in proliferation in palbociclib over the 18-day assay (AEBP2: p-value = 0.002 and JARID2: p-value = 0.0148, unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical analysis.

claim: MTF2 is the most highly expressed and predominant PCL subunit associated with the PRC2 core complex in a variety of contexts.
source: We chose to mutate MTF2 to probe the function of PRC2.1, as it has been shown to be the most highly expressed and predominant PCL subunit associated with the PRC2 core complex in a variety of contexts (Oliviero et al., 2016; Smits et al., 2013).
evidence: This rationale is stated with supporting citations.

claim: SUZ12 has a critical role in bridging accessory proteins with the catalytic core in all known PRC2 complexes.
source: Additionally, SUZ12 has a critical role in bridging accessory proteins with the catalytic core in all known PRC2 complexes (Petracovici and Bonasio, 2021).
evidence: This function is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib when compared with wild-type cells in a 9-day quantitative Crystal Violet assay (MTF2∆ IC50 = 1.033 µM, wild-type IC50 = 0.3936 µM).
source: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib when compared with wild-type cells in a 9-day quantitative Crystal Violet assay (MTF2∆ IC50 = 1.033 µM, wild-type IC50 = 0.3936 µM) while JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive than wild-type (JARID2∆ IC50 = 0.2216 µM) (Figure 4F).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figure.

claim: JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive to palbociclib than wild-type (JARID2∆ IC50 = 0.2216 µM).
source: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to palbociclib when compared with wild-type cells in a 9-day quantitative Crystal Violet assay (MTF2∆ IC50 = 1.033 µM, wild-type IC50 = 0.3936 µM) while JARID2∆ cells were slightly more sensitive than wild-type (JARID2∆ IC50 = 0.2216 µM) (Figure 4F).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figure.

claim: MTF2∆ cells displayed resistance to ribociclib and abemaciclib in a competitive proliferation assay.
source: In addition to showing sensitivity to palbociclib, MTF2∆ cells also displayed resistance to, ribociclib and abemaciclib, two CDK4/6 inhibitors that are structurally related to palbociclib, in a competitive proliferation assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ mutants displayed significantly more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib.
source: However, MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ mutants displayed significantly more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib, while palbociclib treatment resulted in significantly fewer JARID2∆ mutants cells in S phase (Figure 4G).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing BrdU incorporation data.

claim: Palbociclib treatment resulted in significantly fewer JARID2∆ mutant cells in S phase.
source: However, MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ mutants displayed significantly more cells entering S-phase in the presence of palbociclib, while palbociclib treatment resulted in significantly fewer JARID2∆ mutants cells in S phase (Figure 4G).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing BrdU incorporation data.

claim: There was no detectable basal increase in markers of apoptosis in the monoclonal knockout mutant cell lines or when cells were treated with palbociclib for 48 hr.
source: There was no detectible basal increase in markers of apoptosis in the monoclonal knockout mutant cell lines or when cells were treated with palbociclib for 48 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), supporting the conclusion that the resistance to palbociclib observed in the MTF2∆ and SUZ12∆ cells was due to the repressive and promoting role the MTF2-containing PRC2.1 and PRC2.2 complexes play, respectively, in the canonical CDK4/6-RB1-E2F pathway.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: There was no change in the bulk levels of H3K27me3 in MTF2∆ and JARID2∆ cells.
source: western blotting of total H3K27me3 levels in three independently generated clones indicated that there was no change in the bulk levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5A), suggesting that any change of phenotype observed in the mutants was due to a change in the localization of this mark and not due to an overall reduction in its abundance.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing western blot data.

claim: SUZ12∆ cells displayed a significant reduction in the H3K27me3 mark (unpaired Student's t-test, p-value = 0.0104).
source: This is in contrast to SUZ12∆ cells, which displayed a significant reduction in the H3K27me3 mark (unpaired Student's t-test, p-value = 0.0104).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical analysis.

claim: PCA analysis of CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq data showed a high percentage of variance between each of the genotypes tested.
source: Primary component analysis (PCA) of our called, reproducible H3K27me3 peaks and transcript abundance from our CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq data, respectively, showed a high percentage of variance between each of the genotypes tested, along with good clustering of repeats of the same genotype and treatments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a shift in the epigenetic and transcriptional landscapes when either MTF2 or JARID2 are absent.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: PCA analysis of RNA-Seq experiment revealed substantial shifts in variance between palbociclib- and Mock-treated samples for each genotype.
source: PCA analysis of our RNA-Seq experiment revealed substantial shifts in variance between palbociclib- and Mock-treated samples for each genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, bottom), suggesting that exposure to palbociclib resulted in changes in gene expression, consistent with previous reports (Ferguson et al., 2023; Lanceta et al., 2021).
evidence: The results section states this finding with supporting citations and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: PCA of CUT&RUN experiment did not reveal large differences in H3K27me3 distribution between palbociclib-treated and untreated samples.
source: However, the PCA of our CUT&RUN experiment did not reveal large differences in H3K27me3 distribution between palbociclib-treated and untreated samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C – top).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: There were no significant changes in the location of H3K27me3 reproducible peaks in the presence or absence of palbociclib.
source: In line with this observation, when we analyzed the change in distribution of H3K27me3 peaks between palbociclib- and Mock-treated cells using DESeq2, we found no significant changes in the location of H3K27me3 reproducible peaks in the presence or absence of palbociclib (data not shown).
evidence: The results section states this finding from DESeq2 analysis.

claim: MTF2∆ mutants are not resistant to palbociclib because MTF2 is required for a transcriptional adaptation to the drug.
source: This suggests that MTF2∆ mutants are not resistant to palbociclib because MTF2 is required for a transcriptional adaptation to the drug, but instead because MTF2 alters expression of genes important for G1/S progression, even in unperturbed cells.
evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the lack of H3K27me3 changes with palbociclib treatment.

claim: A greater number of promoters with significantly decreased H3K27me3 (log2 fold-change [LFC] ±1, adjusted p-value <0.1) were observed in the MTF2∆ compared to JARID2∆ cell lines (5808 vs 1034 promoters, respectively).
source: We observed a greater number of promoters with significantly decreased H3K27me3 (log2 fold-change [LFC] ±1, adjusted p-value <0.1) in the MTF2∆ compared to JARID2∆ cell lines (5808 vs 1034 promoters, respectively).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3.
source: Of these, 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3, 392 were JARID2-dependent, and 629 were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5B, D).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figures.

claim: 392 promoters were JARID2-dependent for H3K27me3.
source: Of these, 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3, 392 were JARID2-dependent, and 629 were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5B, D).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figures.

claim: 629 promoters were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3.
source: Of these, 5149 promoters displayed MTF2-dependent H3K27me3, 392 were JARID2-dependent, and 629 were co-dependent on MTF2 and JARID2 for wild-type levels of H3K27me3 (Figure 5B, D).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figures.

claim: 733 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon MTF2 inactivation.
source: Consistent with the greater change in H3K27me3 signal at promoters in MTF2∆ cells, 733 versus 114 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon MTF2 versus JARID2 inactivation, respectively, with 666 transcripts that were exclusively MTF2-dependent, 47 transcripts that were exclusively JARID2-dependent, and 67 transcripts displaying co-dependence on both MTF2 and JARID2.
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: 114 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon JARID2 inactivation.
source: Consistent with the greater change in H3K27me3 signal at promoters in MTF2∆ cells, 733 versus 114 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon MTF2 versus JARID2 inactivation, respectively, with 666 transcripts that were exclusively MTF2-dependent, 47 transcripts that were exclusively JARID2-dependent, and 67 transcripts displaying co-dependence on both MTF2 and JARID2.
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: 666 transcripts were exclusively MTF2-dependent.
source: Consistent with the greater change in H3K27me3 signal at promoters in MTF2∆ cells, 733 versus 114 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon MTF2 versus JARID2 inactivation, respectively, with 666 transcripts that were exclusively MTF2-dependent, 47 transcripts that were exclusively JARID2-dependent, and 67 transcripts displaying co-dependence on both MTF2 and JARID2.
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: 47 transcripts were exclusively JARID2-dependent.
source: Consistent with the greater change in H3K27me3 signal at promoters in MTF2∆ cells, 733 versus 114 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon MTF2 versus JARID2 inactivation, respectively, with 666 transcripts that were exclusively MTF2-dependent, 47 transcripts that were exclusively JARID2-dependent, and 67 transcripts displaying co-dependence on both MTF2 and JARID2.
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: 67 transcripts displayed co-dependence on both MTF2 and JARID2.
source: Consistent with the greater change in H3K27me3 signal at promoters in MTF2∆ cells, 733 versus 114 transcripts were significantly upregulated upon MTF2 versus JARID2 inactivation, respectively, with 666 transcripts that were exclusively MTF2-dependent, 47 transcripts that were exclusively JARID2-dependent, and 67 transcripts displaying co-dependence on both MTF2 and JARID2.
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: MTF2-containing PRC2.1 complexes affect the deposition of H3K27me3 in the promoter regions of more genes than the JARID2-containing PRC2.2 in HAP1 cells.
source: These results indicate that the MTF2-containing PRC2.1 complexes affect the deposition of H3K27me3 in the promoter regions of more genes than the JARID2-containing PRC2.2, and therefore, are more important for transcriptional repression in HAP1 cells.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the comparative data.

claim: Only ~30–40% of the promoters with significantly changed levels of H3K27me3 were upstream of protein-coding genes.
source: Only ~30–40% of the promoters with significantly changed levels of H3K27me3 were upstream of protein-coding genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while ~80–90% of the significantly differentially expressed transcripts encoded proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: ~80–90% of the significantly differentially expressed transcripts encoded proteins.
source: Only ~30–40% of the promoters with significantly changed levels of H3K27me3 were upstream of protein-coding genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while ~80–90% of the significantly differentially expressed transcripts encoded proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: A complete loss of H3K27me3 signal intensity at CpG islands was observed in the MTF2∆ mutants.
source: We observed a complete loss of H3K27me3 signal intensity at CpG islands in the MTF2∆ mutants, but only a partial loss at these loci in JARID2∆ cells (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing heatmap data.

claim: Only a partial loss of H3K27me3 signal intensity at CpG islands was observed in JARID2∆ cells.
source: We observed a complete loss of H3K27me3 signal intensity at CpG islands in the MTF2∆ mutants, but only a partial loss at these loci in JARID2∆ cells (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing heatmap data.

claim: There was a significant loss of H3K27me3 peaks at CpG islands in MTF2∆ cells (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 20.4, p-value 2.2 × 10−308).
source: When we expanded our findings genome-wide, we found a significant loss of H3K27me3 peaks at CpG islands in MTF2∆ cells (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 20.4, p-value 2.2 × 10−308), compared with JARID2∆, where this loss was much more modest (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 9.8, p-value = 6.5 × 10−7).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The loss of H3K27me3 peaks at CpG islands in JARID2∆ cells was much more modest (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 9.8, p-value = 6.5 × 10−7).
source: When we expanded our findings genome-wide, we found a significant loss of H3K27me3 peaks at CpG islands in MTF2∆ cells (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 20.4, p-value 2.2 × 10−308), compared with JARID2∆, where this loss was much more modest (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 9.8, p-value = 6.5 × 10−7).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical analysis.

claim: MTF2-containing PRC2.1 is required for all H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands.
source: This result is consistent with the interpretation that the MTF2-containing PRC2.1 is required for all H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands, whereas JARID2-containing PRC2.2 is only required to achieve full wild-type H3K27me3 levels at these sites.
evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the comparative data.

claim: JARID2-containing PRC2.2 is only required to achieve full wild-type H3K27me3 levels at CpG islands.
source: This result is consistent with the interpretation that the MTF2-containing PRC2.1 is required for all H3K27me3 deposition at CpG islands, whereas JARID2-containing PRC2.2 is only required to achieve full wild-type H3K27me3 levels at these sites.
evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the comparative data.

claim: 50–70% of human promoters are estimated to contain at least one CpG island.
source: CpG islands are a very common feature of mammalian promoters, with 50–70% human promoters estimated to contain at least one CpG island (Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This estimate is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: MTF2 is required for H3K27me3 deposition at promoters containing CpG islands involved in cell cycle regulation.
source: These results suggest that MTF2 is required for H3K27me3 deposition at promoters containing CpG islands involved in cell cycle regulation and can explain why MTF2∆ cells display a greater change in gene expression than do JARID2∆ cell lines.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the pathway analysis results.

claim: The promoters of both CCND1 and CCND2 had lost H3K27me3 signal and displayed strong transcriptional induction in MTF2∆ cells.
source: When inspecting the results of our CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq experiments, we found that the promoters of both CCND1 and CCND2 had lost H3K27me3 signal and displayed strong transcriptional induction in MTF2∆ cells (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that the increase in these transcripts was due directly to a change in H3K27me3 in their promoters.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: CCND1 and CCND2 were both among the most upregulated statistically significant transcripts within the MTF2∆ cell line.
source: In fact, while CCND1 and CCND2 were both among the most upregulated statistically significant transcripts within the MTF2∆ cell line, their transcription and promoter H3K27 methylation were unaltered in JARID2∆ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The transcription and promoter H3K27 methylation of CCND1 and CCND2 were unaltered in JARID2∆ cells.
source: In fact, while CCND1 and CCND2 were both among the most upregulated statistically significant transcripts within the MTF2∆ cell line, their transcription and promoter H3K27 methylation were unaltered in JARID2∆ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: DESeq2 analysis of H3K27me3 density in MTF2∆ cells displayed a statistically significant 4.3 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3 signal in the promoter region of CCND1.
source: DESeq2 analysis of H3K27me3 density in MTF2∆ cells displayed a statistically significant 4.3 and 2.7 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3 signal in the promoter region of CCND1 and CCND2, respectively, when compared to wild-type H3K27me3 levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3), whereas changes in H3K27me3 levels in the CCND3 promoter were not statistically significant (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to supplementary figures and files.

claim: DESeq2 analysis of H3K27me3 density in MTF2∆ cells displayed a statistically significant 2.7 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3 signal in the promoter region of CCND2.
source: DESeq2 analysis of H3K27me3 density in MTF2∆ cells displayed a statistically significant 4.3 and 2.7 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3 signal in the promoter region of CCND1 and CCND2, respectively, when compared to wild-type H3K27me3 levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3), whereas changes in H3K27me3 levels in the CCND3 promoter were not statistically significant (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to supplementary figures and files.

claim: Changes in H3K27me3 levels in the CCND3 promoter were not statistically significant.
source: DESeq2 analysis of H3K27me3 density in MTF2∆ cells displayed a statistically significant 4.3 and 2.7 log2 fold-decrease in H3K27me3 signal in the promoter region of CCND1 and CCND2, respectively, when compared to wild-type H3K27me3 levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3), whereas changes in H3K27me3 levels in the CCND3 promoter were not statistically significant (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary file.

claim: The regions upstream of all three D-type cyclins contained CpG islands.
source: Indeed, the regions upstream of all three D-type cyclins contained CpG islands, but CCND1 and CCND2 had regions of GC density about seven times larger (7460 and 6003 bp, respectively) than CCND3 (996 bp) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: CCND1 and CCND2 had regions of GC density about seven times larger (7460 and 6003 bp, respectively) than CCND3 (996 bp).
source: Indeed, the regions upstream of all three D-type cyclins contained CpG islands, but CCND1 and CCND2 had regions of GC density about seven times larger (7460 and 6003 bp, respectively) than CCND3 (996 bp) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding with reference to figures.

claim: The promoter of CCND1 contained about twice as many CpG repeats than did CCND2 (575 vs 379).
source: Furthermore, the promoter of CCND1 contained about twice as many CpG repeats than did CCND2 (575 vs 379) and about six times as many CpG repeats as CCND3 (575 vs 95).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: The promoter of CCND1 contained about six times as many CpG repeats as CCND3 (575 vs 95).
source: Furthermore, the promoter of CCND1 contained about twice as many CpG repeats than did CCND2 (575 vs 379) and about six times as many CpG repeats as CCND3 (575 vs 95).
evidence: The results section states this quantitative finding.

claim: The levels of CCND1 and CCND2 mRNA transcripts, but not CCND3, were regulated by MTF2 in a CpG island-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that the levels of CCND1 and CCND2 mRNA transcripts, but not CCND3, were regulated by MTF2 in a CpG island-dependent manner.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the CpG island analysis.

claim: In pooled knockouts of MTF2, EZH2, EED, and SUZ12, an increase in both CCND1 and CCND2 protein levels was observed by western blot, but not for CCND3.
source: In pooled knockouts of MTF2, EZH2, EED, and SUZ12, we observed an increase in both CCND1 and CCND2 protein levels by western blot, but not for CCND3 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures showing western blot data.

claim: No significant change in either CCND1 or CCND2 levels was observed in JARID2 pooled knockouts.
source: Consistent with the results from our CUT&RUN and RNA-Seq datasets, we did not observe a significant change in either CCND1 or CCND2 levels in JARID2 pooled knockouts.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Clonal knockouts of SUZ12∆ and MTF2∆, but not JARID2∆ lines, had increased mRNA and protein levels for both CCND1 and CCND2, but not CCND3.
source: Again clonal knockouts of SUZ12∆ and MTF2∆, but not JARID2∆ lines, had increased mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) and protein levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) for both CCND1 and CCND2, but not CCND3.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: None of the E-type cyclins, CIP/KIP CDK inhibitors, RB1 or E2F proteins displayed significantly altered mRNA transcript abundance in MTF2∆ or JARID2∆ lines.
source: In contrast to CCND1 and CCND2, none of the E-type cyclins, CIP/KIP CDK inhibitors, RB1 or E2F proteins displayed significantly altered mRNA transcript abundance in our RNA-Seq experiment in either MTF2∆ or JARID2∆ lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Treatment of cells for 6 days with GSK126 resulted in a profound reduction in H3K27me3 levels in all cell lines tested.
source: As expected, treatment of cells for 6 days with GSK126 resulted in a profound reduction in H3K27me3 levels in all cell lines tested and increased CCND1 expression in HAP1 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing western blot data.

claim: GSK126 treatment resulted in increased CCND1 expression in HAP1 cells.
source: As expected, treatment of cells for 6 days with GSK126 resulted in a profound reduction in H3K27me3 levels in all cell lines tested and increased CCND1 expression in HAP1 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing western blot data.

claim: GSK126 treatment resulted in a dramatic increase in CCND1 levels in the non-adherent, haploid CML cell line KBM7.
source: Interestingly, in the non-adherent, haploid CML cell line KBM7, from which HAP1 was derived (Carette et al., 2011), we also observed a dramatic increase in CCND1 levels.
evidence: The results section states this finding with a supporting citation.

claim: GSK126 treatment resulted in increased levels of CCND1 in the breast cancer line MDA-MB-231.
source: Additionally, we observed that GSK126 treatment resulted in increased levels of CCND1 in the breast cancer line MDA-MB-231 and the SV40-immortalized monkey kidney fibroblast cell line COS7 (Figure 6D), suggesting that PRC2 activity can repress CCND1 expression in multiple mammalian cell lineages and species.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure.

claim: GSK126 treatment resulted in increased levels of CCND1 in the SV40-immortalized monkey kidney fibroblast cell line COS7.
source: Additionally, we observed that GSK126 treatment resulted in increased levels of CCND1 in the breast cancer line MDA-MB-231 and the SV40-immortalized monkey kidney fibroblast cell line COS7 (Figure 6D), suggesting that PRC2 activity can repress CCND1 expression in multiple mammalian cell lineages and species.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure.

claim: Increased levels of CCND1 was not observed in the prostate adenocarcinoma cell line LNCaP and the immortalized mouse embryonic cell line NR-6 upon GSK126 treatment.
source: In agreement with the context-dependent nature of PRC2 regulation of developmentally important loci, increased levels of CCND1 was not observed in the prostate adenocarcinoma cell line LNCaP and the immortalized mouse embryonic cell line NR-6, illustrating that regulation of CCND1 expression by PRC2 is not observed in all cellular lineages.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Depletion of either SUZ12 and MTF2 in both COS7 and MDA-MB-231 resulted in significantly increased CCND1 expression.
source: Consistent with results from propagation of these cell lines in GSK126, depletion of either SUZ12 and MTF2 in both COS7 and MDA-MB-231 resulted in significantly increased CCND1 expression (Figure 6E), suggesting that MTF2-containing PRC2.1 represses this loci in diverse cell types in addition to HAP1.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing western blot data.

claim: Overexpression of either CCND1 or CCND2 was sufficient to induce resistance to palbociclib.
source: Consistent with the interpretation that the increased levels of D-type cyclins resulted in palbociclib resistance observed in MTF2∆ cells, overexpression of either CCND1 or CCND2 was sufficient to induce resistance to palbociclib (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Increased association of CCND1 with FLAG-tagged CDK6 was observed in both SUZ12∆ and MTF2∆, but not JARID2∆, knockout cells.
source: We observed increased association of CCND1 with FLAG-tagged CDK6 in both SUZ12∆ and MTF2∆, but not JARID2∆, knockout cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that elevated levels of D-type cyclins indeed drive the formation of active CDK4/6 complexes.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to supplementary figure showing co-IP data.

claim: MTF2∆ mutant cells maintained a higher ratio of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated RB1 at each concentration of palbociclib tested compared to WT or JARID2∆ cells.
source: However, compared to WT or JARID2∆ cells, MTF2∆ mutant cells maintained a higher ratio of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated RB1 at each concentration of palbociclib tested (Figure 6F).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figure showing western blot data.

claim: The increased levels of CCND1 and CCND2 in MTF2∆ cells increases CDK4/6 kinase activity, driving cells into S-phase.
source: This result suggests that the increased levels of CCND1 and CCND2 in MTF2∆ cells increases CDK4/6 kinase activity, driving cells into S-phase (Figure 4G).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the RB1 phosphorylation and BrdU incorporation data.

claim: MTF2-containing PRC2.1 antagonizes G1 progression by repressing expression of the D-type cyclins CCND1 and CCND2 in certain cellular contexts.
source: In total, our results suggest that MTF2-contiaing PRC2.1 antagonizes G1 progression by repressing expression of the D-type cyclins CCND1 and CCND2 in certain cellular contexts.
evidence: This conclusion is stated as the main finding of the study.
